Hasbro and Fathom Entertainment are bringing the original 1986 animated film The Transformers: The Movie back to the big screen this fall. The movie will receive a limited theatrical run in 4K resolution starting on September 17 to celebrate the 40th anniversary of the franchise. Fans can look forward to seeing the beloved characters return to cinemas across the United States with some entirely new surprises waiting at the end.

A brand new post credits scene awaits longtime returning fans

During a recent panel at San Diego Comic-Con, Hasbro revealed that this release will feature an exclusive addition. For the first time ever, audiences will get to see a brand new post credits cinematic chapter of the story. This extra scene was created specifically for the upcoming theatrical event to give both new and returning viewers a fresh reason to experience the classic story in a crowded room.

The theatrical run includes exclusive merchandise and premium format options

For those wanting a more immersive watch, the film will also play in the premium 4DX format.

Fans heading to the theaters can also grab exclusive collectible items while supplies last. Participating locations will sell specially designed popcorn buckets and unique drinkware to mark the anniversary. Between the updated 4K visuals, the fresh story content, and the physical collectibles, this fall event aims to be a definitive celebration for anyone who grew up watching the iconic robot factions battle it out.

articles.title: AAPL stock rallies 15% as investors favor AI caution and welcome price increases
articles.subtitle: Apple stock slid significantly downwards in the wake of the WWDC keynote, with some attributing that to disappointment in the company’s AI announcements.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
Apple stock slid significantly downwards in the wake of the WWDC keynote, with some attributing that to disappointment in the company’s AI announcements.

While we disagreed with that analysis, investors do now seem to be welcoming the company’s caution when it comes to AI spending, with the stock rallying 15% since that June low …

The company’s shares slid 4% the day after the keynote, but there were a number of macroeconomic factors affecting a wide range of stocks at the same time, including US strikes against Iran after the downing of an American helicopter.

The stock has rallied even more substantially since then, pushing it back into record territory. Bloomberg believes that AI is a factor in this, albeit somewhat indirectly. It suggests that investors are growing increasingly skeptical about AI spending by other companies and says that Apple’s more cautious approach is now seen as a positive.

The stock’s reversal reflects rising unease about the prospects for heavy spending on AI paying off, with Apple’s decision not to participate in the data center arms race increasingly being viewed as an asset, rather than a liability, even though its AI offerings have repeatedly frustrated investors.

“There’s a battle in the market, and right now Apple is benefiting because it isn’t in the storm that the rest of the AI trade is in,” said Mark Bronzo, chief investment strategist at Rye Strategic Partners. “People are concerned about what kind of return hyperscalers could get from their AI spending [and] as a result, investors have gravitated back to Apple as a steady-eddy name without those risks. ”

articles.title: Indie Dev Surprised To Find People Are Using His Old Game To Play Undertale Online
articles.subtitle: It’s possible that you’ve heard of a game called Crashphalt, but it’s highly unlikely that you ever actually played it.
articles.author: Kotaku
articles.content:
It’s possible that you’ve heard of a game called Crashphalt, but it’s highly unlikely that you ever actually played it.

That might sound harsh, but don’t blame me; blame Undertale, as the indie dev behind Crashphalt recently revealed that while its free-to-play game “didn’t set the world on fire” when it released on Steam in 2018, it suddenly began to experience a second life in 2023 after being “taken over” by the mod Undertale Together, which lets people play Toby Fox’s landmark role-playing game Undertale in local co-op.

As spotted by Automaton, the indie dev behind Crashphalt, Cold Pressed Games, explained in a thread on the r/IndieDev subreddit that they noticed “something strange” when they checked the game’s Steam reviews a couple of months ago. The “something strange” in question was that Crashphalt had suddenly earned an “Overwhelmingly Positive” review score on Steam, and that almost every review since 2023 directly mentioned Undertale.

For context, between Crashphalt’s release in October 2018 and December 2022, the game received a grand total of 20 reviews on Steam. From January 2023 to today, almost eight years since Crashphalt’s release, the game has garnered 552 more reviews—and almost all of them make some kind of reference to Toby Fox’s 2015 indie hit Undertale.

Naturally, Cold Pressed Games was more than a little perplexed, so they did a little digging. Turns out, a local multiplayer mod for Undertale, named Undertale Together, was indirectly to blame. Undertale Together allows folks to play Undertale …together, but it only supports local co-op. However, on December 2, 2022, a YouTube account named AMMARO73 posted a video detailing a way to use Crashphalt as a sort of proxy to enable online co-op in Undertale via the Undertale Together mod and Steam Remote Play.

Mystery solved, but what does Cold Pressed Games think about all this? As they explained, in response to the many Crashphalt Steam reviews questioning whether or not the developer was happy about how “no one cares about their game and only uses it to mod other games,” they’re cool with it.

“I actually don’t mind what Crashphalt has become. I’ve long since moved on to other projects, so I think its really cool to see that the game has found a second life,” stated Cold Pressed Games on Reddit. “ Undertale came out around the same time I was getting into game dev, and was incredibly inspiring to me. So I think its really cool that it’s found a way to impact the community even if in a small way and act as a way for friends to play the game together.”

Hopefully this leads in some way to people actually playing Crashphalt, as it honestly looks pretty fun, like a cute mix between TowerFall and Nidhogg. At the very least, perhaps the attention can be used to shine a light on the “other projects” that Cold Pressed Games is currently working on.

articles.title: Apple tech will underlie Ford’s EV platform ↦
articles.subtitle: Apple Newsroom: Apple and Ford today announced that Apple Maps will be integrated directly into Ford’s upcoming Universal Electric Vehicle (UEV) Platform through Apple’s new MapKit for Automotive SDK. …
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
Apple Newsroom:

Apple and Ford today announced that Apple Maps will be integrated directly into Ford’s upcoming Universal Electric Vehicle (UEV) Platform through Apple’s new MapKit for Automotive SDK. Coming to Ford’s UEV Platform in 2027, this integration will deliver a beautiful and easy-to-use navigation experience powered by Apple Maps directly to the vehicle’s displays. Road-level Maps information will also enable Ford’s Latitude AI team to build a seamless hands-free driving experience.

This shouldn’t come as a huge surprise: Ford CEO Jim Farley has been bullish on CarPlay and the UEV project was previously headed up by Doug Field 1, who spent several years at Apple both on the Mac hardware team and, more significantly, leading up the abandoned car effort.

This integration is interesting, though, because of the lukewarm reception of CarPlay Ultra in the automotive industry. The new “MapKit for Automotive SDK”, which as far as I can tell is being announced in this press release, seems more like the Android Automotive approach of building in support at a low level, though here it’s predominantly focused on navigation rather than providing the full stack for the car. Here’s how Apple describes it:

This integration is made possible by Apple’s new MapKit for Automotive SDK, which allows automakers to embed and customize Apple Maps. The SDK also enables automakers to deliver a cohesive navigation experience for drivers that is consistent with the look and feel of their vehicles, and provides road-level information to help automakers build hands-free driving experiences.

I also appreciated this little tidbit nestled at the very end of the press release:

In addition to the integration of Apple Maps into Ford’s UEV Platform, CarPlay will continue to be available on Ford vehicles, providing drivers with a safe and smart way to use their iPhone in the car.

Translation: Eat it, GM.

Field announced his departure earlier this year. ↩

articles.title: Running Simulators Inside Claude Code for Mac
articles.subtitle: Claude Code has a new simulator button. Claude Code’s Mac desktop app has added Apple simulator support, and although it’s billed as “iOS Simulator Support,” it actually works with any iOS, iPadOS, visionOS, or watchOS simulator you have installed.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Claude Code has a new simulator button.

Claude Code’s Mac desktop app has added Apple simulator support, and although it’s billed as “iOS Simulator Support,” it actually works with any iOS, iPadOS, visionOS, or watchOS simulator you have installed.

The process of setting up a simulator is simple. A new button with an iPhone icon appears when you open an existing project. Click it and a new iPhone simulator pane opens to the right by default. However, clicking on the name of the simulator reveals a list of every available simulator. You can also run multiple simulators at once, but that immediately made my aging M1 Max Mac Studio start to chug a little.

With access to your running app, Claude Code is more effective at debugging UI bugs.

Once you have the simulators that you want open, simply ask Claude Code to run and test your app, and it gets to work, building the app, installing it in the simulator, opening it, and poking around. I loaded up a simple word game I’ve been playing with, and after a few minutes, Claude Code found a UI bug while controlling the simulator. I asked it to fix the issue, which it did, then tested and committed. My testing has been limited, but so far it looks like a simple, effective loop.

It’s also worth noting that Claude Code is running the simulator directly inside the Claude app. This is not computer use, meaning windows aren’t going to be opening and getting in your way as you work on something else. All in all, the addition of the simulator, like the inclusion of an in-app sandboxed browser a couple of weeks ago, is a great update to Claude Code.

Intelligent Home app notifications

Have you ever been sick of your family using your electronics without asking, and thought 'boy, I should put spikes and a taser on this thing'? If the answer is yes, then you're like Redditor ConroyyJenkinss (presumably no relation to Leroy), who has done just that.

Taking to the Steam Deck subreddit, they recently announced "I Built a Security System for My Steam Deck", and it is one heck of a security system.

steamdeck from r/SteamDeck/comments/1v6osor/i_built_a_security_system_for_my_steam_deck

"I got sick of my family always draining my Steam Deck's battery and not recharging it", ConroyyJenkinss said, so they decided to 3D print a spiky case they made in Blender to snap onto the side of the device. That makes it tough to hold.

From there, they rigged up a Raspberry Pi with a speaker to an object detection camera, and wrote a Python script to "play a goofy audio clip" and set off a taser fitted to the top of the Deck after a few seconds. No, they don't say what the audio is. As far as I can tell, the taser is just there to scare would-be battery thieves, as it can't make contact from its perch above the Steam Deck.

You might be wondering why the Redditor didn't simply put a password on the Steam Deck and leave it at that. Jenkinss says, "This minimises the risk of them touching my Steam Deck at all, they are forced to ask for permission now."

Naturally, this defense mechanism isn't designed to actually serve its purpose. It's a goofy experiment that is done just to see if it can be done. Jenkinss even acknowledges in the comment section that disarming the taser and taking the spike case off is a hassle. I suppose there's more justification to keep the device safe, with it recently seeing a huge price increase.

One redditor in the comments section calls it "hostile architecture for gadgets", and now I'd love to see a tournament of the most abrasive and over-the-top defence mechanisms against the painful experience of having your family waste your battery life.

articles.title: Review: Xteink X3 is the little e-reader the world’s not quite ready for
articles.subtitle: An e-reader magneted to the back of a smartphone, just as the prophecy foretold. The market for small e-readers has been booming lately.
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
The market for small e-readers has been booming lately. Earlier this year, Jason took a look at the Xteink X4, a pint-sized reading device that was about as light and small as they come. But those maniacs at Xteink weren’t done yet: they followed it up with the $79 X3, which is unbelievably even lighter and smaller.

I wouldn’t blame you for wondering if there’s such a thing as too small and light—at 3.84 inches by 2.51 inches (and just 0.2 inches thick) the X3 is still larger than, say, a credit card, but not by much. The screen itself measures just 3.7 inches, more than half an inch smaller than the X4’s 4.3 inch, but its 259 ppi resolution still makes it plenty easy to read on. 1 At that size it’s little imposition to take it with you wherever you go. Easy to lose? Maybe. Easy to love? Yes.

For one thing, this small size unlocks at least one capability that the X4 couldn’t fully deliver upon—the ability to stick to the back of your phone. Like the X4, the X3 has a MagSafe-compatible magnet in its rear case and it fits just about perfectly on the back of my iPhone 17 Pro, nestled below the camera plateau.

However, the magnet is not particularly strong, and it lacks the secondary stabilizing magnet that you see on official MagSafe accessories, meaning it wobbles around a bit. I wouldn’t call it a super secure connection, but it’s pretty good if you’re just slipping it in and out of a pocket. Just be aware that it probably will come loose.

Like the X4 before it, the X3 features a pair of rocker switches on the front for a total of four possible buttons. But they’ve opted to skip the X4’s side mounted rocker switch in favor of a single buttons on each side. There’s also an on/off switch at the top (plus a recessed button used for resetting the device). And with all of that, they somehow managed to continue to fit a microSD slot in the top. The bottom left corner also has a little set of holes for a lanyard or wrist strap.

The one casualty of the smaller X3, however, is the port. The X4 was big enough to accommodate a USB-C connector, but the X3’s thin profile makes that impossible. Instead, there’s a pogo-pin USB cable that connects to four magnetic contacts on the reader. Is this a step back? Strictly speaking, yes.

Using a proprietary connector is a bummer in the year 2026, especially because it means having to keep track of a single-use cable. That said, once you get the X3 up and running, the only real need for the connector is charging, and the battery on this thing lasts a very long time. (I’ve yet to run it down in several weeks of usage.

) Just remember to make a note of where you stow that cable for the point months down the road when you do need to charge it and find yourself wondering whatever happened to it.

As with the X4, the X3 lacks any sort of screen lighting, meaning that it’s strictly a “read in bright light” device. But don’t worry, because Xteink has already unveiled a new X4 Pro with the company’s first lit screen. 2

All in all, I found the X3 very comfortable to read on, whether attached to my iPhone or not. The side buttons work great as page-turners, and the screen is high-contrast and sharp enough to make text render very clearly. All in all, it’s a great reading experience—if you take into account one major caveat.

Soft where?

The elephant in the room for the Xteink X3 is the software. Xteink ships the X3 with its own built-in firmware which, by all accounts, has improved since the first version. But I can’t really tell you, because upon opening the box and powering up the device, the first thing I did was install Crosspoint, the open-source community-built firmware that has turned this device from a curiosity into a real contender. 3

Unlike a lot of other firmware replacements, Crosspoint is super easy to install; you can do it right from a web browser. While it’s not fully free of technological hurdles, I’d say that most people comfortable using an e-reader or updating their iPhones will be able to handle the process with few problems. And the benefits are manifold.

Crosspoint goes beyond simply turning this into a functional device and into one that is actually fun to use. It’s got a straightforward, easy to navigate interface that makes it simple to do everything from reading to loading books (accomplished via a web-based interface). For those who like to tweak their reading setup, there are plenty of configuration options, everything from screen orientation to hyphenation and, yes, custom fonts loaded via the SD card.

Even the onscreen keyboard that you need to use for various configuration tasks is pretty solid for what’s available—on par with navigating via an onscreen keyboard with a game controller, in my opinion. I wouldn’t want to have to type in my Wi-Fi password every time—and you don’t, because it saves it for you—but one time was fine.

There are also a bunch of other features that might appeal to those who want to take reading to the next level. For example, support for Open Publication Distribution System (OPDS) standard means that if you want to host your book library on your own server, you can point your reader at that and download any of the books you already own directly to your device. There’s also support for KOreader sync to help keep your place between supported devices. 4

Crosspoint has been so successful, in fact, that the team at Xteink has smartened up and started collaborating. (This after a brief moment when it looked like the company might try to firmware lock its devices.

) Now, not only do the “developer editions” sold directly by the company continue to allow you to install the custom firmware, the company has been working with the Crosspoint team to make sure new devices, like the X4 Pro, will already be supported when they arrive. While Xteink hasn’t quite adopted Crosspoint as the default OS, it’s not far off.

articles.title: macOS 27 Golden Gate: The MacStories Public Beta Preview
articles.subtitle: The public beta of macOS 27 Golden Gate is out today, and I’m sure many of you are wondering whether to take the plunge and give it a try in advance of its official fall release. That’s the question this preview is here to help answer.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
The public beta of macOS 27 Golden Gate is out today, and I’m sure many of you are wondering whether to take the plunge and give it a try in advance of its official fall release. That’s the question this preview is here to help answer.

It’s not my final take on Golden Gate by any means; after all, I’ve only been using it for about a month, and there will be several more turns in the beta cycle between now and the public release. However, I’ve used Golden Gate long enough to help you make an informed decision about whether or not to install the public beta now.

Of course, it’s impossible for me to account for everyone’s unique Mac setups when considering Golden Gate’s stability, but it’s worth reiterating what I’ve said in past previews: modern Apple betas have been consistently stable. That’s to say, the risks of using the public beta are modest. It’s been years since I’ve had a critical app fail or lost data.

I never go into beta season without a backup plan, though. If something goes terribly wrong, I have backups, backups of those backups, and alternate Macs I can switch to in the event of a disaster. I don’t expect to have to go to Plan B, but if you’re going to jump on the Beta Bus, you should have a Plan B, too.

Okay, you’ve been warned. Let’s get to the fun part.

Supported By

Inoreader

Every year’s macOS update is a little different, but Golden Gate is more different than most. Instead of focusing on tentpole features and apps (with the exception of a new Siri app), macOS 27’s updates fall into three broad categories:

refinements to Apple’s Liquid Glass design language,

hundreds of system-level changes intended to improve your Mac’s performance, and

Apple Intelligence, which includes the new Siri app as well as many other AI additions to existing system apps.

It’s been a while since the “Snow Leopard Moment.”

With so many past macOS updates focusing on system apps, it’s refreshing to see Apple take a more holistic system-level approach, which harkens back to how most people remember OS X Snow Leopard. In fact, during WWDC briefings, Apple representatives likened the Golden Gate update to Snow Leopard before anyone in the room even asked about it.

Snow Leopard is remembered as a release that focused on performance over features. The reality is that the update also introduced its fair share of new features, but many were less splashy from a user-facing standpoint. They were under-the-hood updates that made the Mac work better without users having to think about it much. In that sense, Golden Gate has a lot in common with Snow Leopard.

Other than the brand new Siri app, you probably won’t notice that much is different when you first launch the new version. But over time, the changes will reveal themselves, adding up to a whole that – with few exceptions – is greater than the parts.

So let’s take a closer look at how Liquid Glass has evolved, the most significant system changes, and what it’s like to use Siri and other Apple Intelligence updates in Golden Gate’s public beta.

Design

Windows stand out from each other more, and the sidebar runs edge to edge in Golden Gate.

articles.title: Siri will sometimes summarize webpages and videos from within Safari and YouTube apps
articles.subtitle: Although the Siri app refuses to summarize webpages, the intelligent assistant can do so from within Safari. Similarly, it can summarise the content of YouTube videos from within the app – though the exact situation with both appears complex … The Siri...
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
Although the Siri app refuses to summarize webpages, the intelligent assistant can do so from within Safari.

Similarly, it can summarise the content of YouTube videos from within the app – though the exact situation with both appears complex …

The Siri app refuses to summarize URLs

In the first developer beta, the Siri app would not summarise the content of a URL pasted into it. However, it would not explicitly refuse. This behavior changed in beta 2, with an explicit refusal.

A new section in Siri AI’s system prompt now says: “You cannot access content behind a URL. When a user provides a URL and asks you to summarize, read, or extract information from it, inform them that you cannot access web pages. Do not offer follow-up suggestions or workarounds.”

We speculated that this may be a deliberate decision on the company’s part in order to avoid robbing websites of visitors, which would make the web increasingly unsustainable over time.

Siri in Safari and YouTube will sometimes summarize

However, if you are inside the Safari app and ask Siri to “summarize this,” then it will do so at least some of the time. Other times, it will say it’s unable to do so.

It’s the same story inside the YouTube app, where Siri will sometimes summarise a video and other times say it is unable to do so.

9to5Mac’s Take

Given these differing behaviors, it’s not entirely clear what Apple intends the assistant to do in response to these requests. The fact that it’s a developer beta makes it harder still to differentiate intended behaviors from unexpected results, and we can expect further changes in future betas.

When we use the thumbs down feedback response, we can see a report which includes most of the sources used to answer the question. In the case of our own YouTube video, Siri has the 9to5Mac video channel as part of its world knowledge index, so it’s likely to be gathering the information from that. However, there are other occasions when it is very definitely examining the live webpage content – for example, reading a comment that has only just been posted.

We’ve reached out to Apple and will update with any response.

articles.title: Final Fantasy producer explains what's holding back future remakes
articles.subtitle: The Final Fantasy 14 and 16 producer thinks the scale of past entries is too great Related Don't expect more Final Fantasy 7 -level remakes for other entries in Square Enix's legendary role-playing game series anytime soon.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
The Final Fantasy 14 and 16 producer thinks the scale of past entries is too great

Related

Don't expect more Final Fantasy 7 -level remakes for other entries in Square Enix's legendary role-playing game series anytime soon. At least that's what Final Fantasy 14 producer Naoki Yoshida seems to think. During the Final Fantasy 14 Fan Fest in Berlin, Yoshida said he believes that similar scale projects could take even longer than the Final Fantasy 7 remake trilogy — which is really saying something.

The weekend of Berlin Fan Fest was predominantly devoted to revealing new information on Final Fantasy 14 's next expansion — Evercold. But Yoshida discussed the series at large during the Naoki's Room event on July 26. He was joined by special guest Naoki Hamaguchi, director of the Final Fantasy 7 remake trilogy. Naturally, the two eventually discussed the appetite for further remakes.

"I understand the feelings of the players, but you have to think about it," said Yoshida through a translator, "Look at Final Fantasy 6. It's such an incredibly huge game. The scale is just immense. " In his mind, that scale means even more work for the developer who undertakes the project.

"If we did remake those other titles," Yoshida adds, "we'd probably end up having to release them in four or maybe even five installments. "

Image: Square Enix

Such a prospect gives players little hope. If the third entry in the remake trilogy, Revelation, is released in Spring 2027 as planned, that would mean the entire development will have lasted over a decade. Yoshida uses Final Fantasy 6 as an example, probably because of just how grand that game is, with over a dozen party members and a game world that changes drastically. If audiences expect a modern take on the game to look and play like the remake trilogy, the project may not be feasible.

Of course, Square Enix could avoid making the developing cycle of a future remake so massive. The trilogy expands the original with additional story and gameplay elements, with varying success. A more straightforward recreation of older titles, perhaps Final Fantasy 8 and 9, could benefit greatly just from a graphical overhaul and quality-of-life features.

Furthermore, pixel-art games like Final Fantasy 6 could forego a realistic remake entirely in favor of using Square Enix's HD-2D engine, used in the upcoming Final Fantasy Resonance. This would make the scale of the game less daunting, and would likely allow for a remake to be done in a single release.

While the remake trilogy has been a fascinating experiment, Yoshida makes great points as to why it may not be something Square Enix can repeat.

articles.title: Finishing with Fable 5
articles.subtitle: When Fable 5 returned last week, I knew exactly what to throw at it. In February, I started a project out of frustration that likewise ended in frustration, so I put it on the shelf and waited.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
When Fable 5 returned last week, I knew exactly what to throw at it. In February, I started a project out of frustration that likewise ended in frustration, so I put it on the shelf and waited. Five months later, Fable 5 was released, and I knew it was time to finish Editor, a single-view diffing tool for writers rather than developers.

At MacStories, we all write in Markdown, and we’ve used GitHub to share and sync changes among team members since 2015. GitHub is primarily a developer tool, but it’s a fast, reliable way to share our Markdown-formatted article files, too.

We use GitHub the most for the Club MacStories newsletters. Every week, Federico, Devon, Jonathan, and I work on sections for MacStories Weekly and save them to a GitHub repo. That allows any of us to sync the sections locally for reading, editing, and assembling the issue.

The trouble is that as great as Markdown text editors are to write and GitHub is for versioning and syncing, there isn’t a good way to view the changes someone has made to a document. I know because I’ve been looking for a solution for a long time. Some Markdown apps like iA Writer and Bear support versioning or backups, but I’ve yet to find a text editor that can visualize changes made by someone else based on a document’s Git history.

Of course, developers have many ways to track changes to code, including GitHub Desktop, Kaleidoscope, and Git Tower. Code is just text, so those apps can be used by writers, too. However, the process of writing and editing prose is fundamentally different from code. I’ve tried the apps above and others, and it’s just too hard to track changes in the formats development tools use.

This is what it’s like trying to track changes in GitHub Desktop.

We wouldn’t have stuck with GitHub as long as we have if it didn’t work, but that hasn’t made the friction of reviewing changes any less frustrating, especially on Fridays when we send MacStories Weekly. That’s when I had the idea for Editor. I was trying to parse some changes Devon had made to one of my stories with GitHub Desktop, and the friction finally got to me.

One obvious problem was the side-by-side document view many code diffing tools use. I wanted more detail than most diffing tools offer, but in a single, readable view, so I could skim through changes quickly.

Most agent-assisted projects benefit from some up-front research and planning. I knew what I wanted would sink or swim on the design, not the app’s underlying Markdown viewer, so I spent time researching systems for visualizing document edits.

That’s when I came across Upwelling, a multi-author project from Ink & Switch that describes itself as “an independent research lab exploring the future of tools for thought.” In their research paper, the authors described my exact problem:

Unfortunately, version control tools like Git, which are designed for software development, do not suit the needs of writers. Git cannot compare or merge files from WYSIWYG editors such as Microsoft Word… and graphical user interfaces for Git are cluttered with complex concepts such as commit hashes and visualizations of non-linear branching and merging histories.

Ink & Switch’s solution, a prototype collaborative text editor, wasn’t what I wanted to build, but the research behind it was full of interesting ideas that helped me settle on several principles for what would become Editor:

Document changes needed to be visible in a single view that carefully balanced highlighting changes with readability;

A writer should be able to instantly switch from the marked-up version of their document to the clean original and edited final version;

Changes needed to be categorized by filterable types like punctuation, word choice, capitalization, insertions, and deletions to reduce clutter in heavily edited documents;

Change types would be color coded using a side rail system inspired by maps of London’s tube system;

Navigating among individual edits needed to be done by simple j/k keyboard input; and

Global document navigation should employ a mini-map of a document’s edit regions (a feature borrowed from developer IDEs like Xcode) to make it easy to jump from one area of a document to another.

articles.author: Rock Paper Shotgun
articles.content:
BioWearing the crown

Who knows when or if BioWare'll ever be allowed to make a follow-up to Dragon Age: The Veilguard. Whatever ends up being the future of a series EA've left in a rather ambiguous place, a group of Crusader Kings 3 modders have stepped up to make a Dragon Age total conversion that lets folks play out a bit of their own kingdom-battling history in Thedas.

Released late last week as part of a fan-run Paradox modathon, Dragon Age: Thedas at War is a BioWare-flavoured overhaul of CK3 in a similar vein to works folks have made setting up worlds like The Witcher series' Continent in it. Rather than the likes of England, Bavaria, and the Papal States, you fight to sit on the throne of Orlais or a united Ferelden and wage war on the rest of Thedas.

"Ten years after the Second Blight, Thedas is in the midst of healing whilst once again seeing war on the horizon," reads the mod's intro blurb. "Place yourself into the thick of the growing tension as Hassandriel of the Dales, who is trying to ensure his people are not annihilated by Orlais.

Take the reigns of Teyrn Caedmon, who has proclaimed himself as king of Ferelden in his bid to unite everyone under his banner. For those that prefer their politics, join the men and women of Orlais who are always looking to ascend beyond their station. "

As of right now, the mod offers 40 different playable cultures, several Dragon Age-specific religions, and even the option to play as a mage. While the latter's limited to "only those who are outside of a Circle for the time being", it allows you to fling destructive spells at foes or heal allies. Thedas at War also boasts what its creators have dubbed a "Mega Wars system".

It's "designed to make realm-wide wars involve less powerful characters within any given realm", with lesser vassals offered chances to pick sides and either benefit or suffer as a result.

As for the practicalities of playing the mod, you'll only need the base version of Crusader Kings 3 - with the Roads to Power & Royal Court DLCs as optional extras you'll need in order to play as a landless adventurer. The modders "cannot guarantee a stable experience" in multiplayer, so battle friends at your own risk. Going forwards, that same group plan to "continue adding as much content as humanly possible" to Thedas at War, releasing it "in chunks, generally based on complex additions".

We tested the top contenders to find the best Thunderbolt and USB-C docks available to owners of the MacBook Air and MacBook Pro. MacBook Neo users can use any of these docks but are limited to a 10Gbps bandwidth and some display limitations.

Thunderbolt, USB4 or USB-C

The connectors all look the same (technically known as a “Type-C connector”), but there are significant differences, particularly on speed that will determine both data-transfer rate and higher external display refresh rates.

USB-C: 5Gbps or 10Gbps

USB4: 20Gbps or 40Gbps

Thunderbolt 3 and 4: 40Gbps

Thunderbolt 5: 80Gbps / 120Gbps

While a Thunderbolt 4 (TB4) dock will be enough for most casual users, if you can stretch the budget go for a TB5 dock as it will remain current for years, saving you money in the long term, and is backwards compatible with earlier versions and all the way back to USB-C. High-end professionals should always aim for Thunderbolt 5.

The dock needs one (“ upstream “) Thunderbolt or USB-C port for connecting to and charging your laptop (although all recent MacBooks can also power via the MagSafe 3 port), and at least another (“ downstream “) to attach further devices (hard drives, external display, and others).

The USB-C MacBook Neo has just the one data port, with the other reserved for charging. A dock with Power Delivery will greatly expand the entry-level Mac laptop.

If you use your laptop as your principal computer, attaching at least one larger display to create a hybrid desktop/laptop setup, with a keyboard and mouse, will boost your productivity. You can turn that 13in MacBook’s cramped screen real-estate into an iconic iMac-sized 27in or even larger screen by adding an extra display—or connect two or even four large monitors to extend your screen across your whole desk.

You’ll get two or more Extended mode screens (where the screen extends beyond what you can see on the laptop screen) using a Thunderbolt connection (or DisplayPort/HDMI).

Natively over mere USB-C, Macs can connect to only one external display in Extended mode, as opposed to Mirrored mode (which replicates exactly what you get on the laptop screen) but DisplayLink is third-party software that allows some docks to extend to up to four screens on even the most basic Mac.

DisplayLink-supporting docks are also the only way that non-Pro/Max M1 and M2 MacBooks can connect more than one external display.

articles.title: When Find My doesn’t help with separation anxiety
articles.subtitle: I dispense what might be called valuable insight to my friends, as well as in this public forum. My friends know the danger: they might become the topic of a column, which is true for my buddy Jeff, who left a bag containing his passport behind at a hotel.…
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
I dispense what might be called valuable insight to my friends, as well as in this public forum. My friends know the danger: they might become the topic of a column, which is true for my buddy Jeff, who left a bag containing his passport behind at a hotel. Fortunately, he had an AirTag in his bag. That was, however, just the beginning of the journey. (Jeff gave me permission to share his story.) 1

To avoid suspense, I’ll tell you that Jeff doesn’t have his bag back, but will soon.

Grate news

Jeff was out of town on business for a few days—he’s one of those nearly extinct creatures called a “ full-time technology reporter “—and was carrying his passport to Texas not because it’s another country (it hasn’t seceded yet), but because he lacks a Real ID-upgraded driver’s license.

He had a small bag with a few items, including the passport and an AirTag, that he didn’t need to carry, so he used the hotel safe. There have been many articles written about how unsafe hotel safes are, but it feels as if you’re in a decent hotel, it’s still another bar for someone to get through to steal your stuff.

Leaving in a bit of a rush, Jeff didn’t retrieve the bag from the safe. When he realized it wasn’t with him, thousands of miles later, he was peeved. Shouldn’t the “left behind” feature in Find My have alerted him? Find My showed the bag’s location, however. For some reason, it appeared as if it were in the hotel parking lot. I catastrophized with him, assuming it was stolen. He called the hotel, which said it wasn’t in lost and found.

A staff member went out, looked in the parking lot, and said the rough location was a grate—perhaps the bag had been stolen and someone had found the AirTag and dropped it through the slats? Which would imply that a hotel employee or a thief had managed to get into Jeff’s room after he left, open the safe, leave the hotel, and rummage through the bag in the parking lot before absconding.

That wasn’t the case (or valise). The hotel called back the next day. The previous staffer didn’t know, for some reason, that valuable left-behind items were tagged and placed in a safe in the basement, presumably below or near the parking lot. His bag, containing his passport and other items, would be sent back to him.

Jeff’s experience reveals several aspects of the Find My tracking system that you can take advantage of in advance or use if you’ve lost something or left it behind.

Don’t leave me!

Every device and item you have can be set to alert you when you “leave it behind.” I believe this setting is enabled by default, though Apple’s documentation isn’t clear on this point. All of my devices and items have it enabled, and Jeff found it was turned on for all his gear. Here’s how to check:

In a native Find My app, select the device (like a Mac) or an item (an AirTag or other Find My network item) in the list of such things.

On an iPhone, iPad, or Apple Watch, the action sheet appears. On a Mac, click the info (i) icon next to the item’s name on the map. In the upcoming version 27 operating system releases on all platforms, tap or click the More (…) button that appears when you select the device from the list.

Tap or click Notify When Left Behind, which should already show On. (In the 27 releases, tap or click When Left Behind.)

If disabled, turn it on.

Here’s a crucial detail: examine the “Notify me, except at” list. You can manually add to this set of locations (tap or click New Location). However, it primarily grows when you’re notified by an item or device being left behind, and then you tap or click in the notification to ignore it at that location. You are presented with the option to just exclude that item or device from that location or all of your equipment.

It’s very easy to approve that exclude-all button. (Jeff did not; his list didn’t include the hotel.) This can be convenient when you’re at a hotel, a friend’s house, or another location for a few days or frequently, and sometimes leave Find My-tracked stuff there. But once you ignore the location, you won’t get notified in the future. You can modify the list by hand, too.

Jeff may instead have been tripped up by the safe acting as a Faraday cage—a metal mesh or box that shields electromagnetic signals from passing through. The AirTag and other Find My items use Bluetooth to broadcast a rotating identifier at regular intervals. 2 If the safe blocked that signal, Jeff’s iPhone lost contact with the AirTag the moment the bag went in—a few days before he left.

Over at Snazzy Labs, Quinn Nelson has a great in-depth look at the changes coming to Apple’s Game Porting Toolkit with macOS 27 this fall. Paired with Metal 4, it’s a real leap over what’s possible today, and Nelson showcases the difference well.

Thanks to the upcoming update, Nelson was able to use CrossOver, a Windows-to-Mac compatibility layer that allows PC games to be played on a Mac, to spotlight some impressive numbers on games ranging from Red Dead Redemption to the recently released 007 First Light.

Not all games Nelson tried showed the same leap in performance, but that’s true on compatibility layers like Proton on the Steam Deck, too. What’s remarkable is that it’s all done in software and as Nelson points out, the advent of coding agents like Codex and Claude may help bring more PC games to Mac using the Game Porting Toolkit by reducing the porting costs.

Nelson also makes a pitch for an Apple gaming device. I agree with him that more than ever, the pieces, right down to a hardware-focused incoming CEO, are all there for such a device, and I remain optimistic. However, I’ve made the case for such a device for years now to no avail. Still, whether or not Apple builds gaming hardware itself, watch the full video above. articles.title: Apple’s new Foundation Models explained: on-device AI, cloud AI, and everything in between

articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
During the WWDC26 keynote, Apple announced its third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), comprising five models, some of which are local, some of which are cloud-based, and one of which lives in Google’s servers running on Nvidia chips. Here’s a breakdown of how that will work.

A bit of background

When Apple first announced its foundation models in 2024, the lineup included an on-device language model with roughly 3 billion parameters, and “a larger server-based language model available with Private Cloud Compute and running on Apple silicon servers,” as the company put it at the time.

Private Cloud Compute was an ambitious undertaking, as it aimed to deliver cloud-based AI capabilities while preserving the same privacy guarantees users expect from on-device processing.

For this reason, keeping everything in-house was essential. Private Cloud Compute ran in Apple data centers, on servers powered by Apple silicon. Even so, its privacy guarantees could be independently verified by third-party security researchers.

However, as Apple struggled to get its AI aspirations off the ground, the company partnered with Google to use Gemini as the backbone of its new AI efforts, the results of which it announced earlier this week during the WWDC26 keynote.

Apple’s new foundation models

The third generation of AFMs includes five models: AFM 3 Core and AFM 3 Code Advanced, which are on-device models, and AFM Cloud, ADM 3 Cloud (Image), and AFM 3 Cloud Pro, which are server-based. The D in ADM 3 Cloud (Image) stands for diffusion, a technology we’ve covered in the past here.

Except for AFM 3 Cloud Pro, all other models were built to run on Apple silicon devices. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, meanwhile, runs on NVIDIA GPUs hosted in Google Cloud.

This was made possible afer Apple extended its Private Cloud Compute architecture to third-party infrastructure for the first time, “while maintaining Apple’s powerful security and privacy protections,” according to the company.

As for the models themselves, here’s a breakdown of each one, as explained by Apple:

AFM 3 Core, the next generation of our 3-billion-parameter dense model that delivers a step up in quality. AFM 3 Core Advanced, our most powerful on-device model. It’s natively multimodal, enabling helpful features like expressive voices and higher-accuracy dictation.

Built on cutting-edge Apple research, this 20-billion-parameter model uses a sparse architecture, activating just 1 to 4 billion parameters at a time depending on the request. AFM 3 Core Advanced is unlocked by and optimized for our most capable Apple silicon systems. AFM 3 Cloud, our server-side workhorse, optimized for speed, efficiency, and performance.

ADM 3 Cloud (Image), for image generation and editing, which unlocks advanced photo-editing tools, the all-new Image Playground, and more. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, our most capable server-based model, which powers our most demanding use cases, like agentic tool use and complex reasoning.

articles.title: New Baldur’s Gate 3 Mod Has Given Me All The Excuse I Need To Play The Game Again
articles.subtitle: Baldur's Gate 3 Dragon Age: Origins A Baldur’s Gate 3 modder has breathed new life into this three-year-old game by making it feel like an even older game: Dragon Age: Origins.
articles.author: Kotaku
articles.content:
Baldur's Gate 3 Dragon Age: Origins

A Baldur’s Gate 3 modder has breathed new life into this three-year-old game by making it feel like an even older game: Dragon Age: Origins. First spotted by PC Gamer, the True Third Person Camera mod by Relysia adds a realistic, over-the-shoulder third person camera, putting the action right up in your face.

According to the mod’s description, “the camera stays at a fixed distance to keep the close perspective,” adding even more immersion to the already detailed-as-shit game. Relysia has uploaded a short video demoing the mod so you can see it in action.

Relysia said that they’re pleased the mod has gotten so much attention, and they’ve released a second video that compares the game’s original camera with their mod so players can see the difference. (If you’re looking at the mod and wondering how it’s any different than playing BG3 with a controller, give that second video a look because the differences are quite stark.) Relysia also said that a more detailed breakdown of the mod is coming that’ll include how it works in combat.

It’s rare that a simple technical mod like this is enough to awaken the RPG demons that have lain dormant in me since, well, when Baldur’s Gate 3 first came out. I sank hundreds of hours into that game across several characters and eventually reached the point where I felt I had seen enough.

But this mod is scratching at an itch I didn’t know I had, even though I’m not really looking for a hit from the Dragon Age nostalgia pipe. I enjoyed Dragon Age: The Veilguard, have mourned what EA has done to that team at BioWare, and am looking forward to what some of the remnants of that team are working on with The Concierge.

I don’t need a mod that makes BG3 feel more like a Dragon Age game than it already does. But I guess I’m also looking to spend another 100 hours in a familiar place with familiar characters, and this mod offers a perspective that’s just novel enough to make the familiar feel fresh.

Discord and Meta are facing new legal battles that take a completely different approach to holding tech companies accountable. Instead of suing these companies for the harmful content people post online, families and legal teams are arguing that the apps themselves are legally defective products. This strategy tries to bypass older internet laws that usually protect social platforms from being responsible for what their users say, focusing instead on how the software is built and designed.

Families sue platforms for bad design instead of published content

For years, a rule known as Section 230 has protected internet companies from being treated as the publishers of user posts. If someone posts something harmful, the person is liable, not the platform. However, new lawsuits against Meta and Discord take a fresh angle. They argue that the underlying design of these apps is inherently dangerous and addictive for younger audiences.

By focusing on strict product liability and design defects, lawyers claim the software acts like a physical product that went to market without proper safety testing. The lawsuits argue that the algorithms push extreme content and keep kids scrolling for hours by design, which directly harms their mental health and leads to severe consequences.

The apps lack basic safeguards to protect their youngest users

The core argument centers on the idea that these companies know exactly how their systems work but refuse to add simple safety features. For example, parents argue that platforms like Instagram and Discord fail to verify user ages properly and ignore obvious signs of problematic use.

These lawsuits claim that the companies could easily include parental controls, limit endless scrolling, or stop notifications late at night. Instead, the platforms use rewards, alerts, and infinite feeds to keep users hooked. The legal filings suggest that these design choices expose children to serious risks, from mental health crises to dangerous interactions with adult strangers online.

These legal battles push for safety changes over corporate profits

The main goal of these cases is not just financial compensation for the affected families. The lawyers involved want to force a fundamental shift in how social apps are built. They believe that treating software as a potentially defective product is the only way to make tech companies put user safety ahead of advertising revenue.

If courts agree that an app can be legally defective, it could change the entire internet landscape. Developers would have to prove their platforms are safe for kids before launching them, just like manufacturers do for toys or cars. Until then, these ongoing cases will keep putting pressure on the biggest names in tech to fix the flaws in their basic designs.

Today, Apple released an update to its Creator Studio subscription with new features across many of the suite’s apps.

Pixelmator Pro now integrates more deeply with Creator Studio’s other apps. While working in Keynote, Pages, and Numbers, you can open an image directly in Pixelmator Pro, edit it, and save the changes back to the source app’s document. Final Cut Camera for the iPhone and iPad has been updated with support for Clean HDMI Out, more flexible ProRes support, and disabling of digital zoom. Motion now supports vector graphics, and Compressor gains Vision Pro features, while Freeform gains shape creation, opening images in Pixelmator Pro, a Dark Mode, folders, and drawing on the Mac. Plus, Pages, Keynote, and Numbers each added a handful of new features.

Meccha Chamelon's community maps were infected with viruses

Meccha Chameleon has proven this year’s biggest surprise hit, clearing over 15 million sales in under a month to become the latest viral phenomenon. Unfortunately, the latest news around the game isn’t particularly positive.

Last week, an independent researcher named Feint discovered that hackers had placed viruses inside certain user-created Steam Workshop maps. Once launched, community maps like Laser Tag Neon would open an invisible command prompt window that downloaded malicious software. This style of attack is called a malware dropper.

Specifically, it would install a Remote Access Trojan (RAT) on affected systems, giving the attacker the ability to remotely control compromised PCs. The researcher recommended that those who played the affected maps should perform a full malware scan immediately and check their Documents and temporary folders for suspicious. bat files.

The map Laser Tag Neon was removed a few days after Feint’s blog post went up, but additional infected maps, like Chroma Grid Arena, were uploaded in its place. In response, Meccha Chameleon developers lemorion_1224 and Haganeiro put out version 3.1.0, which patched the vulnerability out of the game. However, in the process of removing the hack, the developers’ PC was hit with the virus, which a hacker used to take over Meccha Chameleon ’s 100,000-member Discord.

“While fixing the issue of malware embedded in a MOD map, a system engineer’s PC got infected with malware,” an X post from lemorion_1224 reads. “After that, the hacker bypassed the engineer’s two-factor authentication on Discord, altered the server permissions, and banned all the staff members.

” The PC in question has since been wiped, so it can’t be used to edit the game’s files or add additional exploits. “The perpetrator who hijacked the Discord is likely to issue various statements moving forward, so please refrain from clicking any suspicious links or following any dubious instructions they provide. ”

A few hours ago, the developers were able to get access to the channel back after contacting Discord. “All hackers who had become admins have been fully banned. The server’s highest privilege account has been changed to a different one from the hijacked account, so it is safe.” The game’s developers rolled out update 3.3.1 this morning, which “further strengthened virus protection.”

It’s unknown how many users were affected by the issues, but the exploit may have been in the game for some time. A July 8 Steam review reads: “Game poses a super severe security risk. A friend of mine hosting a game had his computer hacked and someone was trying to take control of his system while we were playing.” The validity of this review hasn’t been confirmed, but the symptoms described match the virus description quite closely.

Although the virus only affected players accessing custom maps, and it appears to have been resolved, this isn’t the first time that Steam games have come loaded with malware. Just two months ago, Valve removed a free horror game, Beyond The Dark, which was stealing users’ data and cryptocurrency. Several other similar cases eventually prompted the Federal Bureau of Investigation to look into the issue, and the organization set up a webpage to collect information.

articles.title: App report: Adding a shelf to my Mac
articles.subtitle: Just ahead of WWDC 2026, Jason Snell noted that he gets a lot of pitches about Mac apps, attributing the sudden boom in macOS offerings to vibe coding aided by artificial intelligence.…
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
Just ahead of WWDC 2026, Jason Snell noted that he gets a lot of pitches about Mac apps, attributing the sudden boom in macOS offerings to vibe coding aided by artificial intelligence. Regardless of how apps are getting built — be it with AI tools or the more conventional developer kits that Apple offers — it’s certainly true that a lot more macOS apps seem to be popping up, extending the capabilities of your hardware. And some of those apps deserve a little extra attention.

And that’s what I’m hoping to do with these app spotlights for Six Colors. We’ll profile some interesting new apps for the Mac (and maybe the odd iOS offering every now and again), and explain why you might want to give it a download.

Do you have an app you’d like to bring to my attention? Simply drop me a line at apps@sixcolors.com with a brief description of your app, and we’ll take it from there.

With that housekeeping out of the way, here’s what I’ve been downloading lately.

Park Shelf

Cleanliness may be next to godliness, but for most of us, our Mac screens are an unholy mess. Open windows clutter up the view, adding another layer of complication to multitasking. An app called ParkShelf from Digital X Design looks to bring some order to the chaos with a handy place for storing open windows instead of placing them in the dock or relying on your Mac’s App Switcher to jump between windows.

Instead, ParkShelf features a floating bar you can position anywhere on your screen (though there is an option to pin it to a specific area if you prefer). That way you need to call up a particular window, it’s just a matter of heading over to where you’ve stashed it in ParkShelf and summoning what you need. The rest of the time, you’ve got a clean, uncluttered workspace so that you can focus on the task at hand.

I’ve been trying out the free version of ParkShelf, where you can store up to three different windows at any one time. For unlimited storage, you’ll need to pay a one-time fee of $6.99 for the Pro version. In addition to the unlimited storage, the Pro version also gives you the ability to customize a hot key that sends an open window into ParkShelf’s waiting arms. (In the free version, option-P serves as the default hot key.)

For my purposes, ParkShelf works best when I’m focusing on a specific project. If I’m on a writing assignment, I can use the app to stash a window of notes, a browser page I’m using to research the topic, and data sheets in PDF form while I type away in my text editor. When I need anyone of those windows, I can turn to ParkShelf to look something up, but otherwise, those windows are out of sight and out of mind.

I’d like it better if I could store multiple web pages or notes, but ParkShelf seems to treat each app as its own window. For instance, even when I have web pages open in Safari for multiple windows instead of tabs, ParkShelf stores the whole kit and caboodle. Still, the free version of Park Shelf is certainly worth trying out if you’re looking for a way to better manage all the open windows on your screen.

Other apps

ScrollPods lets you control scrolling on a Mac by tilting your head. The free utility works with 3rd-gen AirPods as well as any AirPods Pro, AirPods Max and Beats Fit Pro models. Install the app, turn on a switch, and a tilt of your head lets you scroll through emails, web pages and other windows. Mastering just the right tilt takes a little bit of practice, but this is a pretty clever accessibility tool that takes advantage of an accessory you probably already have on hand.

Sleepr is a $5 app that serves as a sleep timer that lives in your Mac’s menu bar and lets you time shutdowns after 15-, 30-, 60- and 120-minute intervals; you can also have your Mac go to sleep at a very specific time. The 3.0 release adds Liquid Glass support, recurring bedtimes that automatically start themselves, a floating alert that can even appear over full-screen apps, and a live menu bar countdown.

Senqu Image Converter is a $5 image utility that lets you convert among JPEG, PNG, HEIC, TIFF and PDF files. The recent 1.2 update added the ability to drop images onto a preset in the full window for instant conversions, while dropping a file now immediately starts the conversion process using current settings.

Apple was roundly criticised back in 2024 for using concept videos of features it was unable to demo.

articles.title: First Look: macOS Golden Gate Public Beta
articles.subtitle: Let’s just get this out of the way: I liked macOS 26 Tahoe. I liked it because it marked the first time in years where Apple seemed to embrace the fact that Mac users deserve productivity improvements, not just syncing up with whatever (often useful, yes)...
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
Let’s just get this out of the way: I liked macOS 26 Tahoe. I liked it because it marked the first time in years where Apple seemed to embrace the fact that Mac users deserve productivity improvements, not just syncing up with whatever (often useful, yes) new features were being introduced to iOS.

I didn’t like the interface changes, especially the way the redesign handled toolbars and sidebars. It actually felt like macOS dodged a bullet by being treated as an afterthought, because pouring more Liquid Glass atop macOS would have made the situation even worse. But over the last summer, I got used to the interface offenses and instead focused on all the improvements.

Turns out that at least some of my friends and colleagues decided that Tahoe’s interface offenses were too great to bear, and despite all those tasty new productivity boosts, they would sit this one out and hope that Apple came to its senses with macOS 27.

Good news for them: While they’ve spent a year without Apple’s first native clipboard history, Shortcuts automation and AI access, and an improved Spotlight, their upgrade to macOS 27 Golden Gate will net them last year’s features as well as a host of other improvements, all wrapped in an interface that is an unequivocal improvement over what Tahoe wrought.

To those folks, welcome back to the current OS version. To those of us who spent a year floating on the glassy surface of Tahoe, welcome to Golden Gate. Available today as a Public Beta and arriving on every Apple silicon-based Mac this fall, it’s an update I’m not going to have to spend a year apologizing for liking.

Design takes a step forward

The fact that there are more design changes in macOS than any of Apple’s other 27 updates speaks volumes about how broken many of the Tahoe design decisions were. Apple describes the design as “even more refined,” because in Apple marketing-speak, broken features are never remedied or fixed—past features are just improved. The truth is, Apple has rolled back numerous missteps and made changes to others to mitigate the issues they caused.

Floating glass sidebars inset from window edges—a choice that made sense metaphorically, but looked awful—are gone, essentially reverted to their previous design, sitting at the left edge of windows, with a darker background for contrast and colored icons to boot.

Toolbars, one of the most important interface conventions of macOS, were flattened and ghostly in Tahoe. In Golden Gate, they pick up better shading and are more legible, though (strangely) the toolbar in inactive windows offers more contrast and legibility than in active ones! In Photos, toolbars are actual bars, not horizontal areas of floating glassy buttons—which means the system no longer has to attempt to add shading behind those areas in order to improve legibility. They’re just legible.

In Golden Gate, windows generally just feel… a bit more square. Apple has made window corners more consistent, and not having the curved corners of the sidebar right inside the curved corners of the window edge also helps make it feel a little less like you’re under the tyrannical rule of the Circle King.

Icons look better across the board in Golden Gate, probably because of a new layered icon compositing approach Apple is taking across its platforms. Unfortunately, apps that dare stick any of their extremities out of the mandated squircle shape are still put in a featureless gray box of shame, which makes it harder to identify icons, especially in appearance modes like Clear and Tinted that remove color as an identifier.

To hear Apple tell it, users are split on the transparency effect of Liquid Glass: some people despise it, and some people can’t get enough of it. As a result, all of Apple’s OS 27 updates introduce a slider—it’s in the Appearances pane of Settings on macOS—that lets you customize the transparency from sort-of-mostly-transparent to sort-of-mostly-opaque.

Given that this update rolls back a lot of Apple’s decisions from a year ago, I’m inclined to believe that there really are two camps when it comes to Liquid Glass. Giving users an option to adjust the setting is probably fine, though I’ve currently got the slider right in the center. We’ll see how that goes.

Siri AI takes the Spotlight

Siri has been a part of the Mac experience for a decade now, arriving on the platform five years after it debuted on the iPhone. While I’m sure that many Mac users have embraced it over the years, it has always been an afterthought at best for me. When I’m sitting at my Mac, I’ve got a keyboard and trackpad to get my job done, so I don’t generally feel the need to talk to my computer.

And while you’ve been able to type to Siri for a while now… well, the other problem with Siri has always been that Siri’s results are rarely as useful as the results of typing those words into a search engine or some other tool.

In macOS Golden Gate, as with all the other OS 27-era releases, Apple has upgraded Siri to become Siri AI, with LLM-derived features that promise much better results. On top of that, Apple has finally done what it should have done long ago and merged Siri and Spotlight, so there are no longer two separate “type to find things” interfaces on the platform.

The result is… still a work in progress, at least so far. Siri AI is a beta feature inside a beta operating system. Betas within betas. First off, it’s a struggle to remember that Siri is actually useful and I should take advantage of it. Years of training myself never to consider Siri have to be untrained, and that’s going to take some time.

Mods as a means of cross-promotion?

Released back in 2018, Crashphalt is a free and eccentric multiplayer game in which players do ground-pounds to send out seismic ripples, striving to punt each other off-screen. It's got an "overwhelmingly positive" Steam user review reception, as of writing, but that's not entirely a judgement on its quality. You see, Crashphalt is a hit today partly because you need it to run an online multiplayer mod for Toby Fox's wonderful RPG Undertale.

Of Crashphalt's 555 currently existing user reviews, the vast majority were written over five years after release, and either totally disregard or cruelly dunk on Crashphalt. An example: "10/10 Funny Undertale game, will never play this."

It all seems rather hard on Crashphalt's creator, RetroSpecter. It makes me think of cuckoos. I am picturing a sparrow striving to feed a wildly overweight and utterly insatiable Toriel. And yet, RetroSpecter isn't fussed about their game being reduced to an unofficial Undertale co-op patch, commenting that "Undertale came out around the same time I was getting into game dev, and was incredibly inspiring to me.

" It makes me curious to read about other games that have enjoyed a freak resurgence because they've become necessary for a mod to work.

You can read RetroSpecter's full story on Reddit. "Back in the 2018, I released my first game on Steam for free, Crashphalt," they begin. "It was a little local multiplayer platform fighter in the vein of games like Towerfall and Samurai Gun.

"And while it didn't set the world on fire, it let me learn the ropes of game dev from start to finish, led me to make many friends that I still keep up and work with, and is one of the many stepping stones that led me to working on games full time. These days I don't about Crashphalt too much. But every once and a while I revisit the steam page to see if anyone is still playing."

It was during one of those irregular check-ins that RetroSpecter noticed the user review boom and mysterious glut of Undertale references. A bit of digging led them to Depa's Undertale Together, a local co-op mod that adds new co-op-specific battle mechanics and puzzles. Undertale Together doesn't support online play by itself, but players have figured out a workaround that involves dragging the Crashphalt game files into Undertale, then renaming the Undertale.exe.

The choice of Crashphalt for this purpose appears random. "I dunno why they chose Crashphalt," RetroSpecter comments. "The only requirement for the hack is that the has Remote Play enabled, and I guess it does help that Crashphalt is free. But I imagine there are tons of games that fit that bill. Crashphalt was just the lucky game chosen for the honor."

Again, RetroSpecter is philosophical about all this. "I think its really cool that it's found a way to impact the community even if in a small way and act as a way for friends to play the game together," they write. "So as long as Steam doesn't take any issue with how Crashphalt is being used, have fun playing fighting Sans with your friends."

The dismissive tone of certain Steam reviews notwithstanding, I like to think that a few Undertale players found time to play and enjoy Crashphalt, after mining its guts. As a recovering Towerfall enthusiast, I'm quite taken by the shockwave mechanic. It's like trying to catapult another kid off a bouncy castle.

RetroSpecter is obviously cashing in on the story for self-promotion. There's a cheeky little postscript: "Toby Fox. if you read this, let me know if you... like.. wanna make a game together. Thanks."

Still, no act of relative positivity should go unrewarded on this here internet. So let's end with a plug for RetroSpecter's latest game, Draftula, a blend of roguelike and Tetris in which you cobble together a vampire's fortress from a choice of around 50 rooms with adjacency bonuses.

articles.title: Apple Responds to Lawsuit Over Fake Bitcoin Wallet Scam in App Store
articles.subtitle: Apple is facing a new lawsuit from three customers who allegedly lost a combined $1.8 million after falling victim to a fake Bitcoin wallet app in the App Store, according to a complaint filed in California federal court on Friday.
articles.author: MacRumors
articles.content:
Apple is facing a new lawsuit from three customers who allegedly lost a combined $1.8 million after falling victim to a fake Bitcoin wallet app in the App Store, according to a complaint filed in California federal court on Friday.

The complaint alleges that Apple violated California's Consumers Legal Remedies Act and other laws by failing to adequately review and monitor apps distributed through the App Store, despite marketing it as "a safe and trusted place to discover and download apps." Due to these assurances in Apple's marketing, the complaint said the plaintiffs trusted that a Sparrow Wallet app they downloaded from the App Store on iOS was legitimate, when in reality it was a fraudulent spoof designed to steal Bitcoin from users.

Sparrow Wallet is only available on Windows, macOS, and Linux. The popular Bitcoin wallet is not available on iOS, but scammers have released fake lookalike apps in the App Store that can trick users into giving up control of their funds.

"Users found their accounts had been wiped out and their cryptocurrency assets transferred to the scammers' private wallets," the complaint says. "This fraud succeeded precisely because Apple exploited the consumer trust it had deliberately cultivated through more than a decade of marketing the App Store as a uniquely safe and trusted environment."

The plaintiffs James Ramirez, Christopher Ellis, and Jalen Delgado had Bitcoin amounts that were worth approximately $875,000, $840,000, and $120,000 respectively stolen via the app from May to August of 2025, according to the complaint.

Even when victims reported fraud, the lawsuit alleges that Apple often took little to no action, and it says other fake Sparrow apps remain in the App Store.

Sparrow Wallet developer Craig Raw has publicly addressed Apple's slow response to multiple fake versions of his app appearing in the App Store. In a January 2024 social media post, for example, he said "there is still a scam 'Sparrow Wallet' app on the @Apple App Store, despite myself and others having reported it weeks ago."

Last month, Raw said his attempt at protecting users by submitting a "placeholder" app to the App Store that contained marketing screenshots stating that Sparrow Wallet is a desktop app only resulted in his Apple Developer account being flagged for termination due to "dishonest activity." Apple later reversed this decision.

The plaintiffs are seeking damages, including reimbursement of all funds wrongfully lost through the fraudulent Sparrow Wallet app.

Update — July 27 at 5:30 a.m. Pacific Time: In response to our request for comment, Apple said it has taken swift action to remove any apps impersonating Sparrow Wallet on the App Store and to terminate developer accounts associated with those apps.

Apple said developers who suspect that content available on an Apple service infringes on their intellectual property rights can submit a dispute form to Apple's legal department, and customers can report App Store scams or frauds too. Apple says it takes immediate action against apps that do not comply with its guidelines.

Apple previously announced that it terminated 193,000 developer accounts over fraud concerns and prevented over $2.2 billion in potentially fraudulent transactions in 2025.
